#en:
I keep telling myself I am going to stop writing these on company time, but the ship never tells on anyone and the ship is the only one who ever really listens.

Starwharf feels wrong tonight. Not broken exactly just off, like a song half a beat out of time. The lights in the forward cargo spine keep dimming and brightening for no reason, and Jared swears it is just the regulator cycling but I have watched that panel long enough to know when something is talking through our systems. Marcus called it "phantom telemetry" with that Trade Authority shrug of his, like as long as the invoice clears, ghosts can have their own stateroom.

I went through the manifest again at mid shift. Half the crates are marked as obsolete medical equipment destined for some LIST rock and the rest are just as bland, all neat codes and dull words that should make me sleepy. Instead, every time I scroll past that one routing flag, my head aches in the same place behind my eyes. Leah says it is just fatigue from staring at screens but she winces the same way and thinks I do not notice. No one will say it out loud, but we all know there is something riding this ship that is not in the paperwork.

I have been thinking a lot about home. Back on Mars, my mother brewed coffee strong enough to peel hull paint and always kept a little extra for whoever came through the door last. I still make a tiny pot at the end of my shift, even if the beans come from some generic vacuum packed brick and taste like they passed through half the Settled Systems. I pour a cup for myself and leave an empty mug across the table, like she used to for my father when he ran late at the docks. It is a silly ritual, but it makes this rented galley feel less like a cargo container and more like a kitchen.

Last week would have been the festival back in our block, when everyone strung lights between the hab stacks and the kids lit sparklers so bright they wiped out the stars for a moment. We would write the worst parts of the year on scraps of paper, burn them in a metal bowl, and then stay up too late eating whatever our neighbors cooked. Out here, the only lights are status LEDs and warning strobes, and the worst parts of the year are all stored on drives we are paid not to read. I miss the noise most of all. A freighter hum is not the same as a crowd laughing.

Healing is a strange thing in space. We get patched up by med kits and stimulants and keep flying, but the things that hurt do not just vanish because the bruise fades. There are days I can talk about the accident on my last posting without shaking, which I suppose means I am healing, but whenever the ship shutters the same way, my stomach drops and my hands go cold. Healing does not mean forgetting. It just means the wound has learned how to ache quietly instead of screaming every second.

Small things grind at me more than they should. That one locker door in the port corridor that squeaks no matter how much lubricant I feed it. Jared leaving his tools scattered on the diagnostics bench so I have to hunt for a zero wire tester every single time. The galley warmers that somehow turn every UC BattleMeal into something lukewarm and soggy, no matter what the wrapper promises. Leah hums the same four notes when she is anxious, over and over, and tonight she caught herself and went quiet so fast it made me more nervous than the humming.

I heard Marcus arguing on the comm with someone from a Trade Authority office earlier, voice low and clipped. I caught words like "override" and "far edge route" before he noticed I was in the passageway and shut it down. Later, in the mess, he cracked jokes like always but kept checking the corridor cameras out of the corner of his eye. People say the Authority is neutral, apolitical, all that brochure talk. Maybe that used to be true. Lately it feels like we are the middlemen for things nobody wants to admit exist, ferrying debts, secrets, and data that can not be allowed to sit still long enough for anyone to look at it too closely.

Some of the spacers we hauled cargo for back at Neon spoke about a woman who could lift memories clean out of your head, neat as pulling a chip from a socket. At the time I laughed, said Aurora makes people see all kinds of things. Now, with our logs flickering and blank spots in the transit records where there should be nothing but routine, I catch myself wondering if I would even know if someone had taken a piece of me. Maybe that is what scares me most that you can be hurt and half healed and never entirely sure what was lost.

I am going to finish this cup, leave the other one untouched across the table, and pretend my mother is just late from the docks. Tomorrow I will tighten the squeaky hinge again, sort Marcus's tools into proper order, and argue with Leah about whether the flickering lights are a problem or just "atmosphere." The ship keeps moving, the crates stay sealed, and whatever rides in our data channels keeps humming under everything we do. Some wounds, personal or otherwise, are not done bleeding yet.
zh:
我一直告诉自己我上班时间不写这个，可飞船从不告密，而飞船是唯一真正在听的人。

星码头今晚感觉不对。不是坏了，只是不对劲，像一首歌差了半拍。前部货舱脊的灯无缘无故一直忽暗忽亮，杰瑞德赌咒说那只是调节器在循环，可我盯那块面板够久，知道什么时候有什么东西在通过我们的系统说话。马库斯带着他那副贸易管理局式的耸肩管它叫"幽灵遥测"，像只要发票结了，鬼也可以有自己的舱室。

中班时我又过了一遍清单。一半的箱子标着是运往某块独立盟岩石的过时医疗设备，其余的一样乏味，全是整齐的代码和无聊的字，本该让我发困。结果，每次我滚过那个航路标记，我的头就在眼睛后同一个地方疼。莉亚说那只是盯屏幕的疲劳，可她也同样皱眉，只是以为我没注意。没人会说出声，可我们都知道这艘船上载着某种不在文书里的东西。

我近来总想家。在火星上，我母亲煮的咖啡浓得能剥掉船壳漆，还总给最后一个进门的人留一点。我如今在下班时仍会煮一小壶，哪怕豆子来自某块普通的真空砖、尝起来像穿过了半个定居星系群。我给自己倒一杯，在桌子对面留一只空杯子，像她以前给我父亲留的那样，当他码头加班晚归。这是个傻仪式，可它让这间租来的厨房不那么像货柜、更像一间厨房。

上周本该是我们街区那边的节日，那时大家在住舱堆之间拉上灯串，孩子们点亮星火，亮到有一瞬间把星星都盖没了。我们会把这一年的糟糕部分写在纸片上，在一只金属碗里烧掉，然后熬夜吃邻居做的任何东西。在这外面，唯一的灯是状态 LED 和警告频闪，而这一年的糟糕部分全都存在我们被付钱不去读的驱动器里。我最想念的是那噪声。货船的嗡鸣和一群人的大笑不一样。

在太空里，愈合是件怪事。我们用医疗包和兴奋剂把伤补上继续飞，可疼过的东西不会因为淤青消退就消失。有些日子我能谈论上次任职的事故而不发抖，我想那意味着我在愈合，可每当飞船以同样方式震颤时，我的胃就下坠、手就发凉。愈合不意味着遗忘。它只是伤口学会了安静地作痛，而不是每时每刻尖叫。

小事比我该有的更磨我。左舷走廊那扇储物柜门，不管我喂它多少润滑剂都吱嘎。杰瑞德把工具散在诊断台上，害我每次都得到处找零线测试仪。厨房保温器不知怎地把每一份联殖战斗口粮都变成又温又湿的东西，不管包装上承诺什么。莉亚焦虑时总哼同样四个音，一遍又一遍，今晚她发觉自己哼了就飞快安静下来，那比哼声更让我紧张。

早些时候我听见马库斯在通讯上跟贸易管理局办公室某人争吵，声音低而急促。在他注意到我在通道里、掐断之前，我抓到了"越权"和"远端航线"这些词。后来在食堂，他像往常一样讲笑话，可一直用眼角瞟走廊摄像头。人们说管理局中立、不问政治，全是宣传册上的话。也许那曾经是真的。近来感觉我们成了那些没人愿意承认存在之物的中间人，运送债务、秘密，以及那些不能被允许静止太久、免得有人细看的数据。

我们回霓虹城时替一些太空人运货，他们谈起过一个女人，能把记忆干净地从你脑子里取出来，利落得像从插槽里拔出一枚芯片。当时我笑了，说极光酒会让人看见各种东西。如今，我们的日志闪烁，运输记录里本该只有例行事务的地方出现空白，我发觉自己在想：要是有人拿走了我的一部分，我是否甚至能知道。也许那才是最让我害怕的——你可以受伤、半愈合，却永远不完全确定失去了什么。

我要喝完这杯，把对面那杯留着不动，假装我母亲只是从码头晚归。明天我会再把那个吱嘎的铰链拧紧，把马库斯的工具整理归位，和莉亚争论那些闪烁的灯是问题还是只是"氛围"。飞船继续移动，箱子保持密封，而无论在我们数据频道里驰骋着什么，都在我们做的每件事底下继续嗡鸣。有些伤口，个人的或别的，还没止住血。

#en:
Didn't sleep again.

Lights are off in the berth, but my head's still lit like a targeting HUD. Every time I close my eyes I see corridors, breach foam, the haze after flashbangs. There is always someone shouting, even when it's quiet. Back in uniform, they used to call it "operational overstimulation." Out here with the Cohort, we just call it "another night."

I keep thinking about that night on Vesta's dark side, before everything finally broke. The evac never came, comms were jammed, and the temperature in that half-collapsed depot kept dropping. We stacked in close under a busted heat duct, helmets off, armor plates clacking every time someone shivered. Mara Kincaid ended up pressed against my shoulder, knees touching mine, Riya Salazar pinning the other side. We said we were conserving body heat, but we all knew the real reason was that none of us wanted an inch of empty space between us and the next breathing heartbeat. I remember feeling every stutter of Mara's breath, every time Riya's hand flexed near her sidearm. Tight little circle of warmth in a dead place, and all I could think was how connected and how damned exposed I felt at the same time. If a shell had come through that roof we'd all have died in a single, perfect cluster.

Outcast Cohort started that night, we just didn't know it yet.

Elena Ward brought me a "gift" a week after we cut ties with command. We were docked at some forgotten transfer ring, flushing tags and burning serials. She walked up, dropped a brand-new sidearm in my lap, cleaner than anything we'd been issued in months. No requisition forms, no crate logs, no questions. The grip was still warm like she'd been holding it too tight. I knew it hadn't been bought. I also knew better than to ask which armory suddenly turned up short. I just racked the slide, checked the chamber, thanked her. Old discipline gets twisted like that; we still follow the rules, we just write our own now.

Sleep used to be a safe house. Lately it's another AO. I lie down and the mind runs drills I didn't approve. I'm back in that slum block after curfew, tracer fire painting the walls, some officer's voice in my ear saying "minimize collateral" while the targeting overlay paints half the neighborhood as threats. I hear the kid I didn't see soon enough. I hear the doors being kicked in two floors over that weren't on our op order. I remember the smell of burning insulation mixed with whatever passed for dinner in that place. Waking up doesn't make it stop. It just changes the color palette.

The Cohort pretends we're fine after a job. Last month, when we pulled that convoy job clean, the celebrations hit fast and hard. Someone tapped a hidden cache, someone else sliced power to a cargo lounge, and suddenly that concrete bunker turned into a riot. Loud music off a battered speaker, cheap liquor poured into ration tins, Mara dancing like she was trying to unlearn every parade-ground step she'd ever been drilled on. Elena laughed for the first time in months, Riya climbed onto a crate and tried to toast "new loyalties" before she forgot the words. I remember the sound of glasses slamming and boots pounding, voices climbing higher and higher until, just as it felt like maybe we'd burned the ghosts out of us, the power flicked back on and it all evaporated. Next morning the place looked like any other staging area: empty shells, spilled drink, a few blood drops no one remembered earning.

I keep going back further, to something smaller. Before desertion, before rogue orders. Shore leave on some backwater rock, walking patrol off-duty because I couldn't switch it off. I saw a dockworker pop open a sealed crate, palms shaking, slide a couple of high-grade components into his jacket, then reseal the lid like nothing happened. Tiny theft, nothing compared to what we were moving in and out of that system. He looked around once, twice, never saw me. I should've called it in. Instead I watched, fascinated, at how easy it was for him to rewrite his little corner of the universe. No reports, no debrief, just need and nerve. I told myself it was beneath my concern. Maybe it was the first time I realized the rulebook was optional for some people, and that the sky didn't fall when they broke it.

Outcast Cohort lives in that space now. Between the orders we were given and the ones we can live with. Between the warmth of a squad pressed together in the dark and the fear that the person closest to you might be the one to pull the trigger when the next impossible command comes down. We walked away from official command because we were done carrying their secrets. I tell myself that every night, while the threats and violence replay in my head like a briefing I can't dismiss.  

Tomorrow we ship out again. Maybe I'll sleep on the way. More likely I'll sit in the troop bay, watching Mara strip her rifle, listening to Elena argue with Riya over routes, feeling the weight of that "gift" on my hip, and wondering at what point a soldier stops being one, and just becomes another man who learned the wrong lessons a little too well.
zh:
又没睡。

住舱的灯关着，可我的脑袋还亮得像一个瞄准 HUD。每次我闭眼，我都看见走廊、破口泡沫、闪光弹之后的烟霾。总有谁在喊，哪怕在安静时。穿制服那会儿，他们管这叫"作战过度刺激"。在这外面跟着队列，我们只叫它"又一夜"。

我总想起维斯塔背阴面那晚，在一切最终垮掉之前。撤离一直没来，通讯被干扰，那座半塌补给站的温度一直往下掉。我们紧紧挤在一个破了的加热管道底下，摘了头盔，装甲板在谁一哆嗦时就咔咔碰。玛拉·金凯德最后压在我肩膀上，膝盖碰着我的，里娅·萨拉萨尔堵住另一边。我们说我们在保存体温，可我们都知道真正的原因是，我们没人想让自己和下一个呼吸的心跳之间隔一寸空。我记得感觉到玛拉的每一次呼吸停顿、里娅的手在随身武器旁每一次抽动。一个死地方里一小圈温暖的紧密。我满脑子想的都是：我同时感觉那么相连、又那么该死的暴露。要是有一发炮弹穿过那个屋顶，我们会完整地一起死在一个完美的簇里。

流放队列就是那晚开始的，只是我们还不知道。

我们跟指挥部分道扬镳一周后，埃琳娜·沃德给我带来一份"礼物"。我们停靠在某个被遗忘的转运环上，清洗标签、烧掉序列号。她走过来，把一支崭新的随身武器丢在我腿上，比我们几个月来配发的任何东西都干净。没有请购单、没有货箱日志、没有提问。握把还是温的，像她握得太紧了。我知道它不是买来的。我也知道不该问哪个军械库突然短缺。我只是拉了拉滑套、检查了弹膛、谢了她。老纪律就是这样被扭的；我们仍遵守规矩，只是如今自己写规矩。

睡眠曾经是个安全屋。近来它是又一个行动区。我躺下，脑子就跑我没批准过的操练。我又回到宵禁后的那片贫民街区，曳光弹把墙刷亮，某个军官的声音在我耳边说"最小化附带损伤"，而瞄准叠层把半个街区标成威胁。我听见那个我没及时看见的孩子。我听见两个楼层之上那些不在我们行动命令里的门被踹开。我记得烧过的绝缘层的味道，混着那地方算作晚餐的不管什么。醒来并不能让它停下。它只是换了配色。

任务之后，队列假装我们没事。上个月，我们干净地做完那趟运输队活儿时，庆祝来得又快又猛。有人撬开一处隐藏的储藏，另一个人切了货运休息室的电，忽然那座混凝土掩体就变成了一场狂欢。破喇叭里放着响音乐，廉价烈酒倒进配给罐，玛拉跳得像在试图忘掉她练过的每一个阅兵步伐。埃琳娜几个月来第一次笑了，里娅爬上一只箱子，想为"新忠诚"敬酒，还没说完词就忘了。我记得杯子猛砸、靴子重踏的声音，人声越爬越高，直到就在感觉也许我们已把鬼从身上烧掉时，电一恢复，一切就蒸发了。第二天早上，那地方看起来和任何别的集结区一样：空壳、洒出的饮料、几滴没人记得挣来的血。

我总往更远处回，回到更小的事。在逃离之前，在失控的命令之前。在某块穷乡岩石上的岸上休假，休班却还在走巡逻，因为我关不掉它。我看见一个码头工撬开一只密封箱，手掌发抖，把几个高等级部件塞进外套，然后像什么都没发生一样重新盖上盖。小小的偷窃，和我们进出那个星系运的东西比起来什么都不算。他四下看了一次、两次，从没看见我。我本该上报。结果我看着，着迷于他改写自己那一小片宇宙有多容易。没有报告，没有述职，只有需要和胆量。我告诉自己那不关我的事。也许那是我第一次意识到，规则手册对某些人是可选的，而他们破坏它时天并没有塌。

流放队列如今就活在那种空间里。在我们被给的命令和我们能与之共处的命令之间。在一队人紧紧压在黑暗中的温暖，和"离你最近的人可能是下一个不可能的命令下来时扣扳机的人"的恐惧之间。我们走出正式指挥部，因为我们受够了替他们扛秘密。我每晚都这么告诉自己，而威胁和暴力在我脑子里重放，像一份我无法驳回的简报。

明天我们又出航。也许我会在路上睡着。更可能的是，我会坐在运兵舱里，看着玛拉拆她的步枪，听埃琳娜和里娅争航线，感觉腰上那份"礼物"的重量，想知道一个士兵在什么点上不再是士兵，只是另一个把错的教训学得稍微太好的男人。
